title: Computer Fundamentals
tagline: How computers work, from the first machines to today
description: Start here, before any language. Where computers came from, from counting machines and the first electronic computers to the phone in your pocket; why everything inside is binary, and how 8, 16, 32 and 64 bits differ; how text, pictures and sound become numbers, and how a letter gets from a program onto the screen; how logic gates add, how a CPU fetches and runs machine code, and how assembly, the first readable languages and today's languages are built on one another; and what an operating system does. Every lesson has interactive demonstrations and quizzes, and short Python exercises that let you build the ideas yourself.

milestones.title: Where Computers Came From
milestones.blurb: What a computer is, the counting machines and looms before electronics, the first electronic computers, transistors and the personal computer, and the computers of today.

lessons.title: What a Computer Is
lessons.summary: A computer is a machine that follows a list of instructions, very fast and without getting bored. Every computer, from the first one to your phone, has the same four parts - input, processing, memory and output - and all of them are built from switches that are either on or off.

lessons.title: Counting Machines and Looms
lessons.summary: Before electricity, people built machines to count and calculate - the abacus, Pascal's adding machine, Babbage's engines - and a loom that read patterns from punched cards. Ada Lovelace wrote the first published computer program for a machine that was never finished.

lessons.title: The First Electronic Computers
lessons.summary: Between 1936 and 1949 the modern computer was invented - Turing's idea of a universal machine, Zuse's relay computer, Colossus and ENIAC with their thousands of vacuum tubes, and the stored-program design that every computer since has used.

lessons.title: Transistors, Chips and the Personal Computer
lessons.summary: The transistor replaced the vacuum tube, the integrated circuit put many transistors on one chip, and the microprocessor put a whole CPU on one chip. That made computers small and cheap enough for homes - the Altair, the Apple II, the IBM PC - and Moore's law kept them doubling.

lessons.title: Computers Today
lessons.summary: Today's computers - laptops, phones, game consoles, servers - are still von Neumann machines, but with many cores, graphics processors, layers of fast memory, and chips designed around low power. The two main families are x86 (most PCs) and ARM (phones and new Macs).

milestones.title: Binary: The Language of the Machine
milestones.blurb: Why computers use two states, counting in binary, bits and bytes, hexadecimal, negative numbers, and what 8, 16, 32 and 64 bits really mean.

lessons.title: Why Binary
lessons.summary: Computers use binary - only 0 and 1 - because a switch that is either on or off is cheap, tiny, fast and very hard to misread. Ten different voltage levels would be easy to confuse; two are not. Every kind of information can be built from enough 0s and 1s.

lessons.title: Counting in Binary
lessons.summary: Binary works exactly like decimal, but each place is worth twice the one to its right instead of ten times. Read a binary number by adding up the places that hold a 1; write a number in binary by repeatedly dividing by 2 and keeping the remainders.

lessons.title: Bits, Bytes and Bigger Units
lessons.summary: Eight bits make a byte, the unit memory is counted in. Kilobytes, megabytes and gigabytes are multiples of it - with the twist that computers count in powers of 2, so a kibibyte is 1,024 bytes while a kilobyte is 1,000. Bits per second measure speed; bytes measure size.

lessons.title: Hexadecimal
lessons.summary: Long binary numbers are hard to read, so programmers write them in hexadecimal - base 16, with digits 0 to 9 and A to F. One hex digit is exactly four bits, so converting between binary and hex is just grouping bits in fours. Hex is everywhere - colours, memory addresses, error codes.

lessons.title: Binary Arithmetic and Negative Numbers
lessons.summary: Adding in binary is like adding in decimal with only 0 and 1, carrying a 1 whenever a column reaches 2. A fixed number of bits wraps around when it overflows. Negative numbers use two's complement - flip every bit and add one - which lets the same adder do subtraction.

lessons.title: 8, 16, 32 and 64 Bits
lessons.summary: The sizes you hear about - 8-bit, 16-bit, 32-bit, 64-bit - are how many bits a number takes. They decide the largest number that fits and, for a processor, how much memory it can address. 32-bit addresses reach 4 GB, which is why computers moved to 64-bit. Byte order (endianness) decides which byte of a number comes first in memory.

milestones.title: Everything Is Numbers
milestones.blurb: Text as ASCII and Unicode, how a letter reaches the screen, fractions and floating point, colours, images and sound, and files.

lessons.title: Text: ASCII and Unicode
lessons.summary: A computer stores text as numbers - one number per character, from an agreed table. ASCII (1963) gave the 128 characters of English one byte each. Unicode gives every character of every language, and emoji, a number, and UTF-8 stores those numbers in one to four bytes while staying compatible with ASCII.

lessons.title: How Text Gets on the Screen
lessons.summary: When a program prints "Hi", it sends the numbers 72 and 105 to the operating system. A terminal turns each number into a character, looks up its shape in a font, and the shape becomes lit pixels. The screen is just a grid of numbers too.

tasks.title: Draw a letter from its bits

lessons.title: Fractions and Floating Point
lessons.summary: Numbers with a fractional part are stored in floating point - like scientific notation, in binary - with a fixed number of significant bits. Many simple decimals such as 0.1 have no exact binary form, so 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3. Money is safer in whole cents.

lessons.title: Colours, Images and Sound
lessons.summary: A colour is three numbers - red, green and blue light, usually 0 to 255 each. An image is a grid of those colours, and compression makes it smaller. Sound is the air pressure measured tens of thousands of times a second, each measurement a number.

lessons.title: Files and File Formats
lessons.summary: A file is a named row of bytes. Its format is the agreement about what those bytes mean - text, a PNG image, a program. Many formats start with a few fixed "magic" bytes that say what they are, and a hex dump shows a file's bytes as they really are.

milestones.title: Inside the Machine
milestones.blurb: Logic gates, adding with gates, memory, the CPU's fetch-decode-execute cycle, machine code, and the memory hierarchy.

lessons.title: Logic Gates
lessons.summary: A logic gate takes one or two bits in and gives one bit out - NOT, AND, OR, XOR, NAND. Each is a few transistors. Truth tables list every input and output. Every circuit in a computer, including the CPU, is built from gates, and NAND alone is enough to build all of them.

lessons.title: Adding with Gates
lessons.summary: Adding two bits gives a sum bit (XOR) and a carry bit (AND) - a half adder. A full adder also takes a carry in. Chain one full adder per bit and you have an adder for whole numbers, which is the heart of the CPU's arithmetic unit. Subtraction reuses it with two's complement.

lessons.title: Memory: Remembering Bits
lessons.summary: Gates connected in a loop can remember a bit - a latch or flip-flop. A row of them is a register. Main memory (RAM) is billions of tiny cells arranged as a long row of bytes, each with a numbered address. Programs read and write memory by address, and RAM forgets everything when the power goes off.

tasks.title: Numbers in a row of bytes

lessons.title: The CPU: Fetch, Decode, Execute
lessons.summary: A CPU repeats one cycle billions of times a second - fetch the instruction its program counter points at, decode what it means, execute it, and move on. A tiny computer with one register and seven instructions shows the whole idea, including how a loop is just a jump back.

lessons.title: Machine Code
lessons.summary: Machine code is a program as the CPU reads it - instructions encoded as bytes. On x86-64, mov eax, 42 is the five bytes B8 2A 00 00 00 and ret is C3. Each CPU family has its own encoding, which is why programs are built separately for each, and why nobody writes machine code by hand.

lessons.title: The Memory Hierarchy
lessons.summary: Memory that is fast is small and expensive; memory that is big is slow. So computers stack several kinds - registers, caches, RAM, SSD - and keep what is used now close to the CPU. Caches make programs that use nearby data much faster than programs that jump around.

milestones.title: From Machine Code to Modern Languages
milestones.blurb: Assembly, the first readable languages, compilers and interpreters, C and Unix, the family tree of modern languages, and one line of code followed all the way down.

lessons.title: Assembly: Machine Code with Names
lessons.summary: Assembly language writes each machine instruction as a short name - mov, add, jmp - with labels instead of addresses. An assembler translates it, almost one line to one instruction, into machine code. So assembly is not binary, but it is the thinnest possible layer over it, different for every CPU family.

lessons.title: The First Readable Languages
lessons.summary: In the 1950s programmers wanted to write maths and business rules, not registers. Grace Hopper built the first compilers and argued for English-like code; FORTRAN (1957) let scientists write formulas; COBOL (1959) business rules; Lisp (1958) and ALGOL (1960) brought ideas every language still uses; BASIC (1964) brought programming to students.

lessons.title: Compilers, Interpreters and Virtual Machines
lessons.summary: A compiler translates a whole program into machine code before it runs; an interpreter reads the program and carries it out as it goes. Many languages do both - Java and C# compile to bytecode for a virtual machine, Python compiles to bytecode for its interpreter, and JavaScript engines compile the hot parts while running.

lessons.title: C and Unix
lessons.summary: At Bell Labs between 1969 and 1973, Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie built Unix and the C language together. C is close enough to the machine to write an operating system in, yet portable between computers. Unix's ideas and C's syntax shaped nearly every system and language since, including Linux, macOS, Android, Windows and C++.

lessons.title: The Family Tree of Modern Languages
lessons.summary: The languages of today descend from a few ancestors - C's syntax, Simula's objects, Lisp's functions. C++ added objects to C; Python made code read like plain English; Java and C# brought virtual machines and garbage collection; JavaScript took over the web; Rust and Go rethought systems programming. Each one trades speed, safety and convenience differently.

lessons.title: One Line of Code All the Way Down
lessons.summary: Follow print("Hi") from Python down through the interpreter's bytecode, the C code of the interpreter, the C library, a system call into the operating system, the terminal, a font and the framebuffer, to lit pixels - every layer of this course in one journey.

milestones.title: Operating Systems and Modern Computers
milestones.blurb: What an operating system does, processes and threads, virtual memory, files and system calls, booting, and networks and the internet.

lessons.title: What an Operating System Does
lessons.summary: The operating system is the program that runs the computer for every other program - it shares the CPU and memory between programs, gives them files and devices through one safe interface, keeps them from interfering with each other, and starts and stops them. Its core, the kernel, is the only code allowed to touch the hardware directly.

lessons.title: Processes, Threads and Scheduling
lessons.summary: A running program is a process - its code, its memory, and its open files. Inside it, threads are the separate lines of execution. The scheduler shares the CPU cores by giving each thread a short time slice and switching between them hundreds of times a second, which is why many programs seem to run at once even on one core.

lessons.title: Virtual Memory
lessons.summary: Every process sees its own private, enormous row of addresses - virtual memory. The CPU translates each virtual address to a real place in RAM through page tables the kernel keeps, in pages of 4 KB. That keeps processes apart, lets programs use more memory than there is RAM, and makes a bad pointer crash only its own program.

lessons.title: Files, Drivers and System Calls
lessons.summary: A disk only stores numbered blocks; the file system turns them into named files in folders. Drivers let the kernel talk to each kind of device. Programs reach both through system calls - open, read, write, close - and running a program is itself a system call that loads an executable file into a new process.

lessons.title: Booting: From Power Button to Desktop
lessons.summary: When the power comes on, the CPU starts running firmware from a chip on the motherboard (UEFI, once BIOS), which checks the hardware and loads a boot loader from the disk. The boot loader loads the kernel, the kernel starts its drivers and the first process, and that process starts everything else, ending with the login screen.

lessons.title: Networks and the Internet
lessons.summary: Computers send data to each other in small packets, each with an address. IP addresses say where a packet goes, TCP makes delivery reliable and in order, and DNS turns names like example.com into addresses. The web is built on top - HTTP requests and responses carried by those packets - and every layer is still bits on wires and radio waves.
